title: Maharashtra Bans Analogue Paneer for One Year as States Crack Down on Dairy Fraud
excerpt: Over 35% of paneer samples failed state standards, with vegetable oils replacing genuine milk fat in products served without disclosure at restaurants and hotels.
body:
• Maharashtra has imposed a one-year ban on the manufacture, sale, and distribution of analogue paneer after 35.4% of tested samples failed quality standards
  • Analogue paneer, made from vegetable oils and additives instead of milk, was being served as genuine dairy paneer without disclosure in restaurants and hotels
  • Gujarat has imposed a similar ban, and Karnataka is conducting statewide raids and testing paneer samples at food establishments
  • Violators face penalties ranging from six months' imprisonment and a Rs 1 lakh fine to life imprisonment if consumption causes death

Maharashtra has become the second Indian state to impose a sweeping one-year ban on analogue paneer — a cheaper substitute made from vegetable oils and additives — after a year-long surveillance exercise found that more than a third of samples tested across the state failed prescribed food safety standards.

The prohibition, issued through a gazette notification by Maharashtra Food Safety Commissioner Tukaram Mundhe, covers the entire supply chain: manufacture, processing, preparation, packing, storage, distribution, wholesale, and retail sale. Hotels, restaurants, caterers, cloud kitchens, and local eateries are explicitly barred from using, preparing, serving, or stocking analogue paneer in any dish.

What Testing Revealed

The ban follows a year of enforcement that the state's Food and Drug Administration concluded had failed to curb deceptive practices. Of 308 paneer and dairy analogue samples analyzed between April 2025 and March 2026, 109 — or 35.4% — failed state standards. Among these, 79 were classified as sub-standard and 30 were declared unsafe, according to BW Retail World.

Laboratory testing revealed that natural milk fat was frequently replaced with cheap vegetable oils and non-dairy fats. The FDA also found analogue paneer being transported and sold without original packaging, mandatory labels, invoices, batch identification, or traceability documents, making it impossible to trace the source of the products.

"The big question is why fake or duplicate products made with palmolein oil are legally allowed to use dairy names like cheese or paneer. It's like allowing gold-polished brass or aluminium jewellery to use the BIS hallmark logo."

— R.S. Sodhi, Former Managing Director, Amul

Why It Matters for Consumers

Analogue paneer lacks the primary nutritional benefits of genuine dairy paneer — particularly the protein content that millions of vegetarians across India rely on as a dietary staple. The substitute typically contains higher amounts of processed fats and limited quantities of essential vitamins and minerals.

The core consumer concern is deception. Restaurants and hotels across Maharashtra were serving analogue paneer as conventional dairy paneer without informing customers. This practice has been designated an unfair trade practice under Section 24 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.

Penalties are severe. Violations can attract imprisonment of six months and a fine of Rs 1 lakh. In cases where consumption of unsafe food results in death, offenders could face life imprisonment and a minimum fine of Rs 10 lakh.

Multiple States Take Action

Maharashtra is the second state to ban analogue paneer, following Chhattisgarh. Gujarat has also moved against the product, bringing three states into what is becoming a coordinated crackdown on dairy fraud.

In Karnataka, food safety officials have been conducting raids at hotels and other food establishments, collecting paneer samples for laboratory testing. Inspections have reportedly found instances of analogue paneer being used in place of genuine milk-based paneer, and 35% of samples tested showed the presence of vegetable fat, according to NewsfirstPrime. The state has not yet imposed a formal ban but is under growing pressure to follow Maharashtra and Gujarat.

At the national level, a committee has recommended that the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) stop permitting new dairy analogue products altogether. The recommendation calls for no new standards on analogue paneer to be created and for approximately 1,000 existing licence holders to be given time to remove these products from the market.

What to Watch

For Indians traveling home and for the diaspora community that follows food safety debates closely, the enforcement landscape is shifting. Paneer appears in dishes from palak paneer to paneer tikka across restaurants nationwide. The bans in Maharashtra and Gujarat mean establishments in those states must now serve only genuine dairy paneer. Visitors to Karnataka should be aware that enforcement is active even without a formal prohibition.

Jayatheertha Chary, managing director of Mother Dairy, called the Maharashtra ban "a progressive step" that would "strengthen trust in the country's dairy ecosystem." BJP MLA Vikram Pachpute, who raised the issue in the state legislature and pushed for the ban, has called for extending scrutiny to cheese analogues, alleging that consumers face similar deception with processed cheese products.

Whether additional states follow with their own bans will depend on the results of ongoing testing and the FSSAI's national-level response. The existing law permits a prohibition of this nature for a maximum of one year, meaning any permanent solution will require changes to national food safety regulations.
nri_angle: The crackdown on analogue paneer affects NRIs visiting India who eat at restaurants, and highlights food safety standards that diaspora consumers increasingly track across India's food industry.
author: Diaspora Desk
